I’d like you to build a personal blog website.

### Hosting & Repository

This workspace is connected to a GitHub repository, which will be used to host the website via **GitHub Pages**.

Please build the site so that it can be deployed directly to GitHub Pages. Keep the implementation simple, maintainable, and suitable for a personal blog.

### Website Structure

The website should have a main landing page with two primary content categories:

1. **Mainframe**

   * Blog posts about IBM Z, z/OS, mainframe technology, systems administration, and related topics.

2. **Computing & Technology**

   * Blog posts about general computing, technology, programming, history of computing, women in technology, and other technology-related subjects.

The homepage should provide an easy way to browse both categories and discover recent posts.

Each blog post should have:

* A title
* Publication date
* Category
* Tags where appropriate
* Proper formatting for technical content
* Support for code blocks and command-line examples
* A readable, comfortable layout for longer technical articles

### Design & Visual Style

The overall aesthetic should be:

* **Pink**
* **Cute**
* **Girly**
* Visually distinctive and memorable

Think of a **cute personal tech blog**, rather than a generic corporate technology website.

Use a cohesive pink colour palette, with complementary colours for backgrounds, text, cards, links, buttons, and accents. Feel free to incorporate subtle decorative elements, but don't let them interfere with readability.

The design should work well on both desktop and mobile.

### Existing Blog

My old blog is available at:

**return16.blog**

Please inspect/scrape the existing blog to understand:

* Existing blog posts
* Categories and topics
* Writing/content structure
* Useful metadata
* Any content that can be migrated to the new site
* Existing URLs or other information that may be useful

Use the existing blog as a source of content and inspiration, but **do not simply reproduce its old design**. The goal is to create a substantially improved modern version.

Preserve the existing written content where appropriate, while restructuring it to fit the new site's organisation and design.

### Technical Requirements

Please:

* Use a static-site approach that works well with GitHub Pages.
* Client side javascript can be used where appropriate.
* Keep the project structure clean and understandable.
* Store blog posts in an easy-to-edit format such as Markdown.
* Make categories and tags easy to maintain.
* Ensure pages have appropriate metadata and SEO basics.
* Include responsive design.
* Ensure good accessibility and readable colour contrast.
* Optimise the site for reasonable page-load performance.
* Avoid unnecessary dependencies or complicated infrastructure.
* Create an empty html template page that I can copy and write into for future blog posts.

The finished result should feel like a **personal, cute, pink technology blog belonging to someone who works with mainframes**, rather than a generic blog template.

There is a folder in the github repository called 'images' with some background-less images that may be used for decoration and accents on the site.

Use the pixel and sparkle motifs from these images to futher accent the design.

# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

RACF users can be made with the ADDUSER command. Because creating a user is a multiple step process with a lot of different RACF commands involved, creating a user via batch is common.

Protected User IDs
A user created without these segments (without the ability to login) is called a ‘protected uid'[1] or sometimes a ‘functional uid’. Protected ids are often used to own and run started tasks, own certificates, and 481: 482: 483: 484:

It is good practice to break up tasks and applications into separate protected uids and not have them associated with a real user, as that user may become revoked and all the services associated with them will cease to function. Protected uids are non-revokable by time 485: 486: 487: 488:

Creating an interactive user
To create a user that can be logged onto you need to add a TSO segment as below – it is also best practice to give the account details like the users full name, a default security group, and an owner. If these are n 489: 490: 491: 492:

By creating the TSO segments with additional parameters, we can have fields in the TSO login screen auto-populate for the user.

ACCTNUM – must be already defined to RACF in the ACCTNUM resource class and the uid must have read access to it. This can be added with the command: PE <account number> CL(ACCTNUM) ID(<userid>)

TSO(ACCTNUM(<account number>) PROC(<default logon proc>) MAXSIZE(<maximum session size>))

I Cooked a SYSRES!

435:
436:

But before we all start panicking, let me preface this by saying it was on my employers z/D&T (Development and Test) environment – not a client system. No mainframes were hurt (much) in the making of this blog post.

440:

So what happened?

444:

TLDR:

448:

It turns out the SYS1.NUCLEUS dataset can’t have extents allocated, it must be exact in size because it needs to be loaded into contiguous memory at IPL time. This is probably common knowledge for experienced mainframers, but for baby mainframers like me this is completely new information (hence the post about it, I must share this exciting news).

452:

So our system issued the following message upon re-IPL

456:
457:

AWSEMI307I Warning! Disabled Wait CPU 0 = 00020000 00000000 00000000 00000081

458:
462:

And if we go to the IBM z/OS 3.1 Documents and look at the disabled wait codes it tells us exactly that – “Initial program load (IPL) tried to load a module from the SYS1.NUCLEUS data set. The SYS1.NUCLEUS data set or an IEANUC0x or IEAVEDAT member occupies more than one extent.” [1]

466:

I will tell myself that IBM wouldn’t have this documented if people didn’t do it on the regular to make myself feel better.

470:

And now for the long version:

474:

Let’s lay down some facts first.

478:
    479:
  • Our test system runs z/OS from the target libraries of the SMP/E zone it is installed in.
    • 483:
  • Is this a bad thing? Yeah, a little bit.
    • 487:
  • Did I make an inactive copy of the target libraries and apply maintenance to those instead? No way, this is a test system and it is prime cowboy hours over here (yeehaw).
    • 492:

    And thus, my debacle began.

    496:

    I applied maintenance with a standard SMP/E apply job. The job came back and reported that SYS1.MIGLIB ran out of space during the apply. No worries. We’ll increase the size.

    500:

    Usually I do this by making a copy of the dataset into a *.NEW with a larger allocation, maybe I even throw a little secondary space on there so I don’t have to come back later (hint: first mistake). Just because some system datasets can have secondary space, doesn’t meant it’s wise or best practice to do that.

    504:

    I now have my slightly larger SYS1.MIGLIB.NEW allocated. Hooray for me.

    508:

    Now comes the second big no-no of the day. I want to swap my SYS1.MIGLIB.NEW with SYS1.MIGLIB. For datasets with no ENQs against them, I can just rename the original SYS1.MIGLIB to SYS1.MIGLIB.OLD and rename SYS1.MIGLIB.NEW to SYS1.MIGLIB. And the system is (hopefully) none the wiser.

    512:

    Except SYS1.MIGLIB has ENQs on our system – specifically from XCFAS and LLA. That’s the cross-system coupling facility and the library look-aside.

    516:

    I can stop LLA temporarily with a /P LLA console command and start it with an /S LLA, I’ve done it before and the world hasn’t ended, so that’s out LLA ENQ taken care of.
    Next, our LPAR being worked on is a monoplex. So the XCFAS is probably not vital to its existence. But I can’t just stop this one, XCFAS is part of JES a 520:

    Specifically, I found this set of commands:

    524:
    525:

    SETPROG LNKLST,UNALLOCATE
    SETPROG LNKLST,ALLOCATE

    526:
    530:

    Did I read the rest of the article? Of course not, who has time for that (mistake the third). I took my linklist unallocate command and went on my merry way.

    534:

    I stop LLA, I unallocate the entire linklist, I swap the dataset names, then I reallocate the linklist and start LLA back up. And everything seems great so far so I rerun my apply job to get the rest of that maintenance on now there’s enough space.

    538:

    The maintenance fails two more times for out of space in SYS1.LINKLIB and SYS1.NUCLEUS – but that’s ok because I know the workaround I used for SYS1.MIGLIB! Let’s do that two more times and give these datasets loads of secondary space (I’m going to stop counting the mistakes before we get into the double digits, but suffice to say – pleas 542:

    This was around the time I started getting abends all over the place, certain commands weren’t working, it was chaos! Because LLA couldn’t look up the commands I was running in storage – the secondary storage had moved everything around when the dataset expanded to accommodate the new members installed by the SMP/E apply job.

    546:

    So according to some very fast panic-googling I did, this problem can be solved with an /F LLA,REFRESH (a modify refresh of LLA to force it to update the locations of all the members), however that turned out to be a lie and jobs and commands were still abending. A second source I found recommended rebuilding the linklist. No problem, I’ve had a little 550:

    It is at this point that I decide to consult one of my more senior co-workers (you know who you are) who very kindly puts up with my 24/7 dumb questions and breakage of things. I would like to know if there is any way out of this besides an IPL? No there is not.

    554:

    Which circles nicely back to the beginning of this post. Wait State 081.

    558:

    So how do we fix this?

    562:

    I have no way of mounting this SYSRES elsewhere to any of the other LPARs, because they’ve all been set up as copies of this first one and all the SYSRES volumes have the exact name VOLSER name.

    566:

    BUT. That also means I can just pinch one of the other LPARs SYSRES volumes quickly and IPL off that. Huzzah, the LPAR is saved (ish).

    570:

    And now begins the process of making an inactive target copy of the z/OS SMP/E zone. So that we can apply maintenance to that without cooking a second SYSRES. Once we’re ready to build a new one, we can initialize the volume with the dodgy SYS1.NUCLEUS, redeploy a copy of the new target datasets to that, and hopefully nothing else goes sideways.

    574:

    To be continued…?

Customizing viewable columns in SDSF panels

430:
431:


Did you know you can edit which fields are displayed in SDSF, their width, and the order they’re displayed in by default?

435:

To make these changes, you first need two pieces of information: the display group you’re part of and the member name that SDSF is reading its parameters from.

439:
To Find your group
443:

In any SDSF panel, enter ‘WHO' in the command input.

447:

This displays information about your session, such as your user ID, your login PROC, your GRPINDEX, and your GRPNAME (these last two are important, so make a note of them).

451:
To find the sdsf parameter member in use
455:

Issue the MVS command ‘/F SDSF,DISPLAY‘ from SDSF, or the same command without the leading slash if you have an MVS console.

459:

There should be a line beginning with PARMS: that shows the member name and data set location.

463:

The default member is SYS1.PARMLIB(ISFPRM00).

467:

We’ve found the important information, now for the customizing

471:

Go to the location of your ISFPRMxx member and open it for editing (preferably after you’ve saved a backup of it in case you mess up).

475:

If you’re working at a client site, there are probably already groups defined in this member. That’s why we first checked which group we were part of. Find your group in the ISFPRMxx member. It will start with a line similar to ‘GROUP ILPROC(BATCH)‘ (where BATCH is your group name in this 479:

Everything indented beneath this line defines your group’s attributes. If you have any customized fields, they’ll be listed here using ‘nnFIELDS' statements, where nn is the short character name for the SDSF panel being customized.

483:

For example, CKFIELDS customizes the Health Checker panel fields, while HFIELDS customizes the Held Output panel fields. It will appear like this ‘HFIELDS(HFIELD1)' (where HFIELD1 is our example customized display).

487:

The name of the customized display listed here points to a section of FLDENT statements beneath a ‘FLD NAME(n) TYPE(m)' statement (where n is the name you found in the group definition and m is the type of panel being customized).

491:

Below that will be a FLDENT line for every column you want displayed in the SDSF panel table. FLDENT statements follow this syntax ‘FLDENT COLUMN(c),TITLE(t),WIDTH(n)‘

495:

Note: If you want to use a title containing non-standard characters, such as hyphens or spaces, enclose the title (t) in single quotation marks like this ‘…,TITLE('Sample Title')‘

499:

IBM has a handy reference table that lists all available columns and their default attributes.

503:

Reading in the new ISFPRMxx after customizations

507:

Once you’ve updated the fields you want to display, you can read in the new ISFPRMxx member dynamically with the following command

511:
512:

/F SDSF,REFRESH,MEMBER(xx)

513:
517:

The xx refers to the last two digits on your IFAPRMxx member.

521:

Why would we need this?

525:

The main benefit of this feature is that you can control which users are assigned to which groups using SAF.

529:

So you can create custom field layouts that allow users to view only the information they’re permitted to see on an SDSF panel. Or just make a cleaner, less cluttered panel that only has information relevant to your job role.

  • JCL is a staple language for Systems Programmers, and arguably the most important part of any JCL is the job card – we can’t run a JCL without one.

    The reason a lot of people call it a ‘Job card’ (you might also hear other terms like Job statement) is because MVS programming used to be done on punch cards. If you’ve never heard of a punch card, IBM has a nice     history lesson on them.

    To have a valid job card, you need at minimum a job name and the JOB keyword. That would look something like this:

    //SAMPJOB JOB

    But that gives us and JES absolutely no information about the job, which is where the positional and keyword parameters come in. They can be used to provide extra information such as the account that is running the job, who to notify upon job completion, what initiator class the job should use, and many other options [1]. A more realistic job card would be something like this:

    //JOBNUM1 JOB 504,SMITH PAYROLL,
    //        CLASS=X, NOTIFY=&SYSUID,
    //        REGION=0M

    After the job statement, there are two positional parameters: Job accounting information (in our example, that is 504) and the programmer name field (in our example, SMITH PAYROLL). These positional parameters are not required unless your site has made it a rule.
    Then, we get to the Keyword parameters. Unlike the positional, these keyword parameters can go in any order because they all start with ‘keyword=’ and value is provided after. The most commonly used keyword parameters are:

    CLASS – which JES initiator class the job should run under. Available initiators can be checked by going to the SDSF INIT panel. Sites usually assign initiators to specific batches- for example, class L might be for long-running jobs or class O might be for overnight jobs. Check with someone at your site if you’re unsure what your classes are for.

    MSGCLASS – where the job output is printed to. Every system should have a class A by default, which points to the JES spool. If your site has other printers set up you may want to code in a different value.

    MSGLEVEL – the amount of detail in the job output. E.g., MSGLEVEL=(N1,N2). N1 can be a value from 0-2 and N2 can be a value from 0-1 where the higher the number you specify the more detail is provided. More about what exactly these values print can be found here. The system default is (1,1).

    NOTIFY – the UID to notify with a TSO interrupt on job completion or failure this can be hardcoded, e.g., NOTIFY=TSOUSR1 or the &SYSUID variable can be used like in the above example. &SYSUID will substitute in the UID of the user that submits the job.

    REGION – the amount of central or virtual storage your job can use. Often, you will see REGION=0M which means the job is allowed to use as much storage as it needs. If your job does not have enough storage, e.g., if you limit it to REGION=24M and it needs more storage to perform the work, you may see an abend such as ‘S878’.

IBM provides some sample ISPF edit macros in the SYS1.SISPSAMP library. These are useful as is or as a basis for learning to write your own edit macros. Today we will discuss a few of them.

First of all, to use the edit macros we need to ensure that SISPSAMP is allocated. This can be done be including it in our login procedures under the SYSPROC concatenation, or with an ALLOC command. For example:

ALLOC F(SYSPROC) DA(‘SYS1.SISPSAMP’) SHR REU

this is a TSO command, so remember to prefix it with TSO if you are entering it from an ISPF panel. Once they are allocated, edit macros are always called by entering the member name on the command line of your ISPF edit session.

ISRONLY:
Only is an edit macro that combines the functionality of the FIND and EXCLUDE macros. It will display only the lines with the string that you specify. Instead of doing command X ALL;F <string> ALL you can use command ONLY <string>.

ISRBOX:
Box is an edit macro that inserts an box drawn from characters into the open member you are editing. The box’s top left corner will start at your cursor position. It will then reposition your cursor inside of the box so you can begin to enter a note in it. It is useful for highlighting notes for yourself or other programmers.

TSO & ISPF DDnames

But wait… something is different about these two edit macros – apart from their functionality.

If you notice when viewing the members, ISRONLY has a /* REXX */ comment declaration at the top. ISRBOX does not, this is because ISRBOX is a CLIST program. Edit macros can be written in REXX or CLIST, and you will often see a combination of both where CLIST commands are used in a REXX program.

It is important we recognize the difference between the two, because z/OS processes them differently. That is why we allocated SISPSAMP to the SYSPROC concatenation, which can handle running both REXX and CLIST statements. If we were to allocate it to another concatenation like SYSEXEC, which can only process REXX statements, the CLIST macros would return with syntax errors because they are being read as if they are REXX.

This also goes for other ddname concatenations too. If you misallocate a panel to ISPMLIB, when it was supposed to be under ISPPLIB then your panels will most likely not display.

The base ISPF library types are the following:

  • ISPMLIB – Message library
  • ISPPLIB – Panel library
  • ISPSLIB – Skeleton library
  • ISPTLIB – Table input library
  • ISPTABL – Table output library
  • ISPFILE – File tailoring output file
  • ISPLLIB – Load module
  • ISPILIB – Image library

Likewise, TSO has

  • SYSPROC – TSO/E CLISTs and REXX execs
  • SYSEXEC – Only REXX

  • SYS1.UADS is the default dataset listing users that are allowed to use TSO/E [1]. Most sites that have RACF or other security products installed use those products to maintain their TSO/E logon information [2]. For a first time installation of RACF, IBM provides a command called RACONVRT to move users from SYS1.UADS to the RACF database [3]. Before you do this, RACF must be set up to protect TSO resources [4]. Once your site is using RACF to manage TSO users (or if your site is already using it). You can define specific logon procedures for specific users, and allow or disallow users to use certain logon procedures.

    Logon procedures:
    Say we have a given logon procedure we would like to define, TSLOGP in SYS2.PROCLIB.

    At minimum, a logon procedure must have a terminal monitor program (TMP) which is a program that allows a user session to communicate with TSO/E [5]. You may be familiar with the IKJEFT01, IKJEFT1A, and IKJEFT1B TMPs, which can also be used with a JCL job to run commands that you might typically enter in your session in an environment outside of your session- this can keep your screen free so you can keep working if it’s a command that will take a long time to execute.

    Let’s assume the SYS2.PROCLIB(TSLOGP) procedure looks something like this:

    //TSLOGP����� EXEC PGM=IKJEFT01,DYNAMNBR=20
    //SYSIN�������DD TERM=TS
    //SYSPRINT�� DD TERM=TS

    This is a minimal logon procedure [6], it does not define things such as ISPF panels, or other macros or software products. With this logon procedure a user will be limited to working directly from TSO/E. Like a the name of a job in the job card, the first //TSLOGP is the name of our procedure. We are executing IKJEFT01, and the SYSIN and SYSPRINT DDs are both set to the users terminal session. This allows us to enter TSO commands to IKJEFT01 and for it to return the output to our terminal. The DYMAMNBR param refers to how many datasets you can dynamically allocate at the name time [6]. This means datasets that are allocated with the TSO ALLOC command, for example.

    Defining logon procedures to RACF and permitting their use:

    • RDEFINE TSOPROC <your proc name> UACC(NONE) or UACC(READ) – if you want everyone to be able to use it
    • PERMIT <your proc name> CLASS(TSOPROC) ID(<your id>) ACCESS(READ) – if you defined it as UACC none
    • SETROPTS RACLIST(TSOPROC) REFRESH – to refresh TSOPROC. You should now be able to logon with your new procedure.

    Resources:
    [1]     IBM – Content and structure of the UADS
    [2] IBM – Using the RACF data base to maintain TSO/E users
    [3] IBM – Using the RACONVRT command
    [4] IBM – Protecting TSO resources
    [5] IBM – Executing the terminal monitor program
    [6] IBM – Writing a logon procedure

    Many mainframe beginners will be familiar with how to manually purge job outputs from the JES spool one by one – that is, accessing the job status log via SDSF;ST and placing a P against the job entry to be purged. But there are ways we can purge multiple jobs without having to manually enter a P against each job out.
    Most site setups will have automation in place to clear the spool after a given amount of time has passed, but for various reasons we may want to clean up the spool sooner.

    The first way:
    Purging a range. Let’s consider that we a viewing the SDSF;ST panel, and we have a filter of USER ‘our UID’ applied. There is a block of multiple job outputs in a row we wish to clear.
    To purge a range of job outputs we can place a ‘//P’ in the action column of the first block of the job series, and a ‘//’ in the last job of the series. Much like entering block commands in an ISPF edit session. Hitting enter on this will purge the selected job outputs (inclusive) and everything listed between them.

    The second way:
    JES2 Commands. JES2 commands can be entered the same way most MVS commands are; via the console or in any SDSF panel prefixed with a ‘/’. JES2 commands are also prefixed with a ‘$’ to differentiate them from other system and product commands.
    The command ‘/$POJQ,JM=*’ in SDSF, or just ‘$POJQ,JM=*’, will Purge Output from the Job Queue under the Job Mask *. As you may know from other MVS conventions the wild card * can be used to represent ‘any‘. So the above command will purge ALL job outputs. Be careful when issuing this as you may accidentally purge job outputs you didn’t mean to.
    Luckily, $PO offers many different parameters to target only certain subsections of job outputs. These parameters can also be mixed and matched within the same commands to narrow down the subsection even further.

    • $POJQ,JM=JOB12* – Purge job outs beginning with the name JOB12*
    • $POJQ,Q=B – Purge job outs in class B
    • $POJQ,days>2 – Purge job outs that are older than two days

Customizing viewable columns in SDSF panels

07 July 2026
sdsf held-output jes2

Did you know you can edit which fields are displayed in SDSF, their width, and the order they're displayed in by default?

To make these changes, you first need two pieces of information: the display group you're part of and the member name that SDSF is reading its parameters from.

To Find Your Group

In any SDSF panel, enter WHO in the command input.

This displays information about your session, such as your user ID, your login PROC, your GRPINDEX, and your GRPNAME (these last two are important, so make a note of them).

To Find the SDSF Parameter Member in Use

Issue the MVS command /F SDSF,DISPLAY from SDSF, or the same command without the leading slash if you have an MVS console.

There should be a line beginning with PARMS: that shows the member name and dataset location.

The default member is SYS1.PARMLIB(ISFPRM00).

Customizing the ISFPRMxx Member

Go to the location of your ISFPRMxx member and open it for editing (preferably after you've saved a backup of it in case you mess up).

If you're working at a client site, there are probably already groups defined in this member. That's why we first checked which group we were part of. Find your group in the ISFPRMxx member. It will start with a line similar to:

GROUP ILPROC(BATCH)

where BATCH is your group name in this example.

Everything indented beneath this line defines your group's attributes. If you have any customized fields, they'll be listed here using nnFIELDS statements, where nn is the short character name for the SDSF panel being customized.

For example, CKFIELDS customizes the Health Checker panel fields, while HFIELDS customizes the Held Output panel fields. It will appear like this:

HFIELDS(HFIELD1)

where HFIELD1 is our example customized display name.

The name of the customized display listed here points to a section of FLDENT statements beneath a FLD NAME(n) TYPE(m) statement — where n is the name you found in the group definition and m is the type of panel being customized.

Below that will be a FLDENT line for every column you want displayed in the SDSF panel table. FLDENT statements follow this syntax:

FLDENT COLUMN(c),TITLE(t),WIDTH(n)

Note: If you want to use a title containing non-standard characters, such as hyphens or spaces, enclose the title in single quotation marks like this:

...,TITLE('Sample Title')

IBM has a handy reference table that lists all available columns and their default attributes.

Reading in the New ISFPRMxx After Customizations

Once you've updated the fields you want to display, you can read in the new ISFPRMxx member dynamically with the following command:

/F SDSF,REFRESH,MEMBER(xx)

The xx refers to the last two digits on your ISFPRMxx member.

Why Would We Need This?

The main benefit of this feature is that you can control which users are assigned to which groups using SAF.

So you can create custom field layouts that allow users to view only the information they're permitted to see on an SDSF panel. Or just make a cleaner, less cluttered panel that only has information relevant to your job role.

I Cooked a SYSRES!

23 April 2026
zos smp/e

But before we all start panicking, let me preface this by saying it was on my employer's z/D&T (Development and Test) environment — not a client system. No mainframes were hurt (much) in the making of this blog post.

So what happened?

TLDR:

It turns out the SYS1.NUCLEUS dataset can't have extents allocated. It must be exact in size because it needs to be loaded into contiguous memory at IPL time. This is probably common knowledge for experienced mainframers, but for baby mainframers like me this is completely new information — hence the post about it, I must share this exciting news.

So our system issued the following message upon re-IPL:

AWSEMI307I Warning! Disabled Wait CPU 0 = 00020000 00000000 00000000 00000081

SETPROG LNKLST,UNALLOCATE SETPROG LNKLST,ALLOCATE

Did I read the rest of the article? Of course not, who has time for that (mistake the third). I took my linklist unallocate command and went on my merry way.

I stop LLA, I unallocate the entire linklist, I swap the dataset names, then I reallocate the linklist and start LLA back up. And everything seems great — so I rerun my apply job to get the rest of that maintenance on now there's enough space.

The maintenance fails two more times for out of space in SYS1.LINKLIB and SYS1.NUCLEUS. But that's OK because I know the workaround I used for SYS1.MIGLIB! Let's do that two more times and give these datasets loads of secondary space (I'm going to stop counting the mistakes — suffice to say, please don't do this).

This was around the time I started getting abends all over the place — certain commands weren't working, it was chaos! Because LLA couldn't look up the commands I was running in storage — the secondary storage had moved everything around when the dataset expanded to accommodate the new members installed by the SMP/E apply job.

Adding Users to RACF

20 March 2026
racf tso racf-ids userids

RACF users can be made with the ADDUSER command. Because creating a user is a multiple step process with a lot of different RACF commands involved, creating a user via batch is common. RACF commands can be run in batch with the IKJEFT01 program, which allows you to execute TSO commands in batch.

The minimum command you can enter is:

ADDUSER <userid>

You can also list a user once created to view information about them:

LU <userid>

Or delete a user:

DELUSER <userid>

Adding a user with the above command doesn't automatically mean they can log onto a mainframe. To perform certain tasks they need segments and permissions added to their profile, for example:

  • TSO login → needs a TSO segment
  • USS/OMVS usage → needs an OMVS segment

Protected User IDs

A user created without these segments (without the ability to login) is called a 'protected uid' [1] or sometimes a 'functional uid'. Protected IDs are often used to own and run started tasks, own certificates, and similar non-interactive purposes.

It is good practice to break up tasks and applications into separate protected UIDs and not have them associated with a real user, as that user may become revoked and all the services associated with them will cease to function. Protected UIDs are non-revocable by time expiry — they can only be revoked by explicit command.

Creating an Interactive User

To create a user that can be logged onto you need to add a TSO segment — it is also best practice to give the account details like the user's full name, a default security group, and an owner. If these are not specified, defaults from the system ICHRIN03 module or RACF defaults are used.

ADDUSER <userid> DFLTGRP(<groupid>) OWNER(<ownerid>) NAME('<firstname lastname>') PASSWORD(<temp password>)

Adding a TSO Segment

By creating the TSO segment with additional parameters, we can have fields in the TSO login screen auto-populate for the user.

ACCTNUM — must be already defined to RACF in the ACCTNUM resource class and the UID must have read access to it. This can be added with the command:

PE <account number> CL(ACCTNUM) ID(<userid>)

PROC — for the default logon procedure. More on logon procedures can be found in the TSO Logon Procedures and RACF post.

MAXSIZE — the maximum session size the user is allowed to allocate to themselves on logon in KB. The largest possible session size is 2,096,128 KB (approximately 2 GB).

TSO(ACCTNUM(<account number>) PROC(<default logon proc>) MAXSIZE(<maximum session size>))

Adding an OMVS Segment

The same can be done to add the OMVS segment. Like traditional UNIX, a UID of 0 can be set to grant superuser — or any other number for a regular user.

OMVS(HOME(/u/<lowercase userid>) UID(1000) SHARED PROGRAM(/bin/sh))

A Full Example Job to Make a User ID

//ADDUSER JOB ,'add user',
//  MSGCLASS=X,CLASS=A,NOTIFY=&SYSUID
//ADD     EXEC PGM=IKJEFT01
//SYSTSPRT DD   SYSOUT=*
//SYSTSIN  DD   *,SYMBOLS=(EXECSYS,SYMPRINT)
 ADDUSER <userid>                          -
         DFLTGRP(<groupid>)               -
         OWNER(<ownerid>)                 -
         NAME('<firstname lastname>')     -
         PASSWORD(<temp password>)
 ALTUSER <userid>                          -
         TSO(ACCTNUM(<account number>)    -
             PROC(<default logon proc>)   -
             MAXSIZE(2096128))             -
         OMVS(HOME(/u/<lowercase userid>) -
              UID(1000)                    -
              SHARED                      -
              PROGRAM(/bin/sh))
/*

This will make the user ID. We should also do a couple of other things so they can create mainframe datasets under their userid, have secure datasets, and use their OMVS segment.

Defining a Catalog Alias

Add their userid as a related alias to your system's user catalog if it has one (it is best practice). The user's datasets will then be catalogued on the user catalog.

//DEFALIAS EXEC  PGM=IDCAMS
//SYSPRINT   DD  SYSOUT=*
//SYSIN DD *,SYMBOLS=(EXECSYS,SYMPRINT)
   DEFINE ALIAS                       -
          (NAME(&SYSUID)               -
           RELATE('CATALOG.UCATALOG')) -
/*

Protecting Datasets with RACF

Protect their userid-qualified datasets with RACF. Allow other users none or minimal, controlled access to the user's datasets.

//DEFRACF EXEC PGM=IKJEFT01
//SYSTSPRT DD   SYSOUT=*
//SYSTSIN  DD   *,SYMBOLS=(EXECSYS,SYMPRINT)
 ADDSD '<userid>.*' GENERIC UACC(NONE) OWNER(<ownerid>)
 PERMIT '<userid>.*' GENERIC ID(<userid>) ACCESS(CONTROL)
 SETROPTS GENERIC(DATASET) REFRESH
/*

Creating a ZFS for OMVS

Create a ZFS for their UNIX data and make sure to format it. This should be mounted at the user home directory listed in the profile's OMVS segment, which will need to be created if it has not been already. Some systems may have automation set up to automount user directories to USS.

//DEFZFS    EXEC PGM=IDCAMS
//SYSPRINT  DD SYSOUT=*
//SYSUDUMP  DD SYSOUT=*
//SYSIN DD *,SYMBOLS=(EXECSYS,SYMPRINT)
  DEFINE CLUSTER (NAME(<userid>.USER.ZFS) -
     ZFS                                   -
     CYL(5 5) SHAREOPTIONS(3))
/*
//CREATZFS  EXEC PGM=IOEAGFMT,REGION=0M,
//   PARM='-aggregate <userid>.USER.ZFS -compat'
//SYSPRINT  DD SYSOUT=*

References

[1] IBM — Defining Protected User IDs

More about the available parameters that can be used with ADDUSER and the TSO and OMVS segments can be found in IBM's documentation.

Customizing viewable columns in SDSF panels

07 July 2026
sdsf held-output jes2

Did you know you can edit which fields are displayed in SDSF, their width, and the order they're displayed in by default?

To make these changes, you first need two pieces of information: the display group you're part of and the member name that SDSF is reading its parameters from.

To Find Your Group

In any SDSF panel, enter WHO in the command input.

This displays information about your session, such as your user ID, your login PROC, your GRPINDEX, and your GRPNAME (these last two are important, so make a note of them).

To Find the SDSF Parameter Member in Use

Issue the MVS command /F SDSF,DISPLAY from SDSF, or the same command without the leading slash if you have an MVS console.

There should be a line beginning with PARMS: that shows the member name and dataset location.

The default member is SYS1.PARMLIB(ISFPRM00).

Customizing the ISFPRMxx Member

Go to the location of your ISFPRMxx member and open it for editing (preferably after you've saved a backup of it in case you mess up).

If you're working at a client site, there are probably already groups defined in this member. That's why we first checked which group we were part of. Find your group in the ISFPRMxx member. It will start with a line similar to:

GROUP ILPROC(BATCH)

where BATCH is your group name in this example.

Everything indented beneath this line defines your group's attributes. If you have any customized fields, they'll be listed here using nnFIELDS statements, where nn is the short character name for the SDSF panel being customized.

For example, CKFIELDS customizes the Health Checker panel fields, while HFIELDS customizes the Held Output panel fields. It will appear like this:

HFIELDS(HFIELD1)

where HFIELD1 is our example customized display name.

The name of the customized display listed here points to a section of FLDENT statements beneath a FLD NAME(n) TYPE(m) statement — where n is the name you found in the group definition and m is the type of panel being customized.

Below that will be a FLDENT line for every column you want displayed in the SDSF panel table. FLDENT statements follow this syntax:

FLDENT COLUMN(c),TITLE(t),WIDTH(n)

Note: If you want to use a title containing non-standard characters, such as hyphens or spaces, enclose the title in single quotation marks like this:

...,TITLE('Sample Title')

IBM has a handy reference table that lists all available columns and their default attributes.

Reading in the New ISFPRMxx After Customizations

Once you've updated the fields you want to display, you can read in the new ISFPRMxx member dynamically with the following command:

/F SDSF,REFRESH,MEMBER(xx)

The xx refers to the last two digits on your ISFPRMxx member.

Why Would We Need This?

The main benefit of this feature is that you can control which users are assigned to which groups using SAF.

So you can create custom field layouts that allow users to view only the information they're permitted to see on an SDSF panel. Or just make a cleaner, less cluttered panel that only has information relevant to your job role.

So what happened?

TLDR:

It turns out the SYS1.NUCLEUS dataset can't have extents allocated. It must be exact in size because it needs to be loaded into contiguous memory at IPL time. This is probably common knowledge for experienced mainframers, but for baby mainframers like me this is completely new information — hence the post about it, I must share this exciting news.

AWSEMI307I Warning! Disabled Wait CPU 0 = 00020000 00000000 00000000 00000081

23 April 2026
zos smp/e

But before we all start panicking, let me preface this by saying it was on my employer's z/D&T (Development and Test) environment — not a client system. No mainframes were hurt (much) in the making of this blog post.

So what happened?

TLDR:

It turns out the SYS1.NUCLEUS dataset can't have extents allocated. It must be exact in size because it needs to be loaded into contiguous memory at IPL time. This is probably common knowledge for experienced mainframers, but for baby mainframers like me this is completely new information — hence the post about it, I must share this exciting news.

So our system issued the following message upon re-IPL:

AWSEMI307I Warning! Disabled Wait CPU 0 = 00020000 00000000 00000000 00000081

And if we go to the IBM z/OS 3.1 Documents and look at the disabled wait codes it tells us exactly that — "Initial program load (IPL) tried to load a module from the SYS1.NUCLEUS data set. The SYS1.NUCLEUS data set or an IEANUC0x or IEAVEDAT member occupies more than one extent." [1]

I will tell myself that IBM wouldn't have this documented if people didn't do it on the regular, to make myself feel better.

And Now for the Long Version

Let's lay down some facts first.

  • Our test system runs z/OS from the target libraries of the SMP/E zone it is installed in.
  • Is this a bad thing? Yeah, a little bit.
  • Did I make an inactive copy of the target libraries and apply maintenance to those instead? No way, this is a test system and it is prime cowboy hours over here (yeehaw).

And thus, my debacle began.

I applied maintenance with a standard SMP/E apply job. The job came back and reported that SYS1.MIGLIB ran out of space during the apply. No worries. We'll increase the size.

Usually I do this by making a copy of the dataset into a *.NEW with a larger allocation — maybe I even throw a little secondary space on there so I don't have to come back later (hint: first mistake). Just because some system datasets can have secondary space, doesn't mean it's wise or best practice to do that.

I now have my slightly larger SYS1.MIGLIB.NEW allocated. Hooray for me.

Now comes the second big no-no of the day. I want to swap my SYS1.MIGLIB.NEW with SYS1.MIGLIB. For datasets with no ENQs against them, I can just rename the original SYS1.MIGLIB to SYS1.MIGLIB.OLD and rename SYS1.MIGLIB.NEW to SYS1.MIGLIB. And the system is (hopefully) none the wiser.

Except SYS1.MIGLIB has ENQs on our system — specifically from XCFAS and LLA. That's the cross-system coupling facility and the library look-aside.

I can stop LLA temporarily with a /P LLA console command and start it with an /S LLA — I've done it before and the world hasn't ended, so that's our LLA ENQ taken care of. Next, our LPAR being worked on is a monoplex. So the XCFAS is probably not vital to its existence. But I can't just stop it. XCFAS is part of JES and stopping JES is… dramatic.

So I went looking for another way and found a very promising article about the dynamic linklist facility. Specifically, I found this set of commands:

SETPROG LNKLST,UNALLOCATE SETPROG LNKLST,ALLOCATE

Did I read the rest of the article? Of course not, who has time for that (mistake the third). I took my linklist unallocate command and went on my merry way.

I stop LLA, I unallocate the entire linklist, I swap the dataset names, then I reallocate the linklist and start LLA back up. And everything seems great — so I rerun my apply job to get the rest of that maintenance on now there's enough space.

The maintenance fails two more times for out of space in SYS1.LINKLIB and SYS1.NUCLEUS. But that's OK because I know the workaround I used for SYS1.MIGLIB! Let's do that two more times and give these datasets loads of secondary space (I'm going to stop counting the mistakes — suffice to say, please don't do this).

This was around the time I started getting abends all over the place — certain commands weren't working, it was chaos! Because LLA couldn't look up the commands I was running in storage — the secondary storage had moved everything around when the dataset expanded to accommodate the new members installed by the SMP/E apply job.

So according to some very fast panic-googling I did, this problem can be solved with an /F LLA,REFRESH (a modify refresh of LLA to force it to update the locations of all the members). However that turned out to be a lie and jobs and commands were still abending. A second source I found recommended rebuilding the linklist. No problem, I've had a little practice at that… but that didn't fix things either.

It is at this point that I decided to consult one of my more senior co-workers (you know who you are) who very kindly puts up with my 24/7 dumb questions and breakage of things. I would like to know if there is any way out of this besides an IPL? There is not.

Which circles nicely back to the beginning of this post. Wait State 081.

So How Do We Fix This?

I have no way of mounting this SYSRES elsewhere to any of the other LPARs, because they've all been set up as copies of this first one and all the SYSRES volumes have the exact same VOLSER name.

BUT. That also means I can just pinch one of the other LPARs' SYSRES volumes quickly and IPL off that. Huzzah, the LPAR is saved (ish).

And now begins the process of making an inactive target copy of the z/OS SMP/E zone — so that we can apply maintenance to that without cooking a second SYSRES. Once we're ready to build a new one, we can initialize the volume with the dodgy SYS1.NUCLEUS, redeploy a copy of the new target datasets to that, and hopefully nothing else goes sideways.

To be continued…?

[2] IBM, Using Dynamic Lnklst Facility: Using Dynamic Lnklst Facility Safely and Properly

Adding Users to RACF

20 March 2026
racf tso racf-ids userids

RACF users can be made with the ADDUSER command. Because creating a user is a multiple step process with a lot of different RACF commands involved, creating a user via batch is common. RACF commands can be run in batch with the IKJEFT01 program, which allows you to execute TSO commands in batch.

The minimum command you can enter is:

ADDUSER <userid>

You can also list a user once created to view information about them:

LU <userid>

Or delete a user:

DELUSER <userid>

Adding a user with the above command doesn't automatically mean they can log onto a mainframe. To perform certain tasks they need segments and permissions added to their profile, for example:

  • TSO login → needs a TSO segment
  • USS/OMVS usage → needs an OMVS segment

Protected User IDs

A user created without these segments (without the ability to login) is called a 'protected uid' [1] or sometimes a 'functional uid'. Protected IDs are often used to own and run started tasks, own certificates, and similar non-interactive purposes.

It is good practice to break up tasks and applications into separate protected UIDs and not have them associated with a real user, as that user may become revoked and all the services associated with them will cease to function. Protected UIDs are non-revocable by time expiry — they can only be revoked by explicit command.

Creating an Interactive User

To create a user that can be logged onto you need to add a TSO segment — it is also best practice to give the account details like the user's full name, a default security group, and an owner. If these are not specified, defaults from the system ICHRIN03 module or RACF defaults are used.

ADDUSER <userid> DFLTGRP(<groupid>) OWNER(<ownerid>) NAME('<firstname lastname>') PASSWORD(<temp password>)

Adding a TSO Segment

By creating the TSO segment with additional parameters, we can have fields in the TSO login screen auto-populate for the user.

ACCTNUM — must be already defined to RACF in the ACCTNUM resource class and the UID must have read access to it. This can be added with the command:

PE <account number> CL(ACCTNUM) ID(<userid>)

PROC — for the default logon procedure. More on logon procedures can be found in the TSO Logon Procedures and RACF post.

MAXSIZE — the maximum session size the user is allowed to allocate to themselves on logon in KB. The largest possible session size is 2,096,128 KB (approximately 2 GB).

TSO(ACCTNUM(<account number>) PROC(<default logon proc>) MAXSIZE(<maximum session size>))

Adding an OMVS Segment

The same can be done to add the OMVS segment. Like traditional UNIX, a UID of 0 can be set to grant superuser — or any other number for a regular user.

OMVS(HOME(/u/<lowercase userid>) UID(1000) SHARED PROGRAM(/bin/sh))

A Full Example Job to Make a User ID

//ADDUSER JOB ,'add user',
//  MSGCLASS=X,CLASS=A,NOTIFY=&SYSUID
//ADD     EXEC PGM=IKJEFT01
//SYSTSPRT DD   SYSOUT=*
//SYSTSIN  DD   *,SYMBOLS=(EXECSYS,SYMPRINT)
 ADDUSER <userid>                          -
         DFLTGRP(<groupid>)               -
         OWNER(<ownerid>)                 -
         NAME('<firstname lastname>')     -
         PASSWORD(<temp password>)
 ALTUSER <userid>                          -
         TSO(ACCTNUM(<account number>)    -
             PROC(<default logon proc>)   -
             MAXSIZE(2096128))             -
         OMVS(HOME(/u/<lowercase userid>) -
              UID(1000)                    -
              SHARED                      -
              PROGRAM(/bin/sh))
/*

This will make the user ID. We should also do a couple of other things so they can create mainframe datasets under their userid, have secure datasets, and use their OMVS segment.

Defining a Catalog Alias

Add their userid as a related alias to your system's user catalog if it has one (it is best practice). The user's datasets will then be catalogued on the user catalog.

//DEFALIAS EXEC  PGM=IDCAMS
//SYSPRINT   DD  SYSOUT=*
//SYSIN DD *,SYMBOLS=(EXECSYS,SYMPRINT)
   DEFINE ALIAS                       -
          (NAME(&SYSUID)               -
           RELATE('CATALOG.UCATALOG')) -
/*

Protecting Datasets with RACF

Protect their userid-qualified datasets with RACF. Allow other users none or minimal, controlled access to the user's datasets.

//DEFRACF EXEC PGM=IKJEFT01
//SYSTSPRT DD   SYSOUT=*
//SYSTSIN  DD   *,SYMBOLS=(EXECSYS,SYMPRINT)
 ADDSD '<userid>.*' GENERIC UACC(NONE) OWNER(<ownerid>)
 PERMIT '<userid>.*' GENERIC ID(<userid>) ACCESS(CONTROL)
 SETROPTS GENERIC(DATASET) REFRESH
/*

Creating a ZFS for OMVS

Create a ZFS for their UNIX data and make sure to format it. This should be mounted at the user home directory listed in the profile's OMVS segment, which will need to be created if it has not been already. Some systems may have automation set up to automount user directories to USS.

//DEFZFS    EXEC PGM=IDCAMS
//SYSPRINT  DD SYSOUT=*
//SYSUDUMP  DD SYSOUT=*
//SYSIN DD *,SYMBOLS=(EXECSYS,SYMPRINT)
  DEFINE CLUSTER (NAME(<userid>.USER.ZFS) -
     ZFS                                   -
     CYL(5 5) SHAREOPTIONS(3))
/*
//CREATZFS  EXEC PGM=IOEAGFMT,REGION=0M,
//   PARM='-aggregate <userid>.USER.ZFS -compat'
//SYSPRINT  DD SYSOUT=*

References

[1] IBM — Defining Protected User IDs

More about the available parameters that can be used with ADDUSER and the TSO and OMVS segments can be found in IBM's documentation.

+ +

Macro: Insert job card template
About: An ISREDIT macro to insert a job card into a member open in ISPF edit.

/* rexx */
"isredit macro"
"isredit (cur) = cursor"
lineno = cur
line = "//JOBCARD  JOB ,'Name',NOTIFY=&SYSUID.,"
"isredit line_after "lineno" = (line)"

line = "//"

The macro inserts three lines: the JOB statement, a continuation line with common parameters, and a blank comment line. Customize the template to match your site's standard job card parameters.

What's in a Job Card?

JCL is a staple language for Systems Programmers, and arguably the most important part of any JCL is the job card — we can't run a JCL without one.

The reason a lot of people call it a 'Job card' (you might also hear other terms like 'Job statement') is because MVS programming used to be done on punch cards. If you've never heard of a punch card, IBM has a nice history lesson on them.

To have a valid job card, you need at minimum a job name and the JOB keyword. That would look something like this:

//SAMPJOB JOB

But that gives us and JES absolutely no information about the job, which is where the positional and keyword parameters come in. They can be used to provide extra information such as the account that is running the job, who to notify upon job completion, what initiator class the job should use, and many other options. A more realistic job card would be something like this:

//JOBNUM1 JOB 504,SMITH PAYROLL, // CLASS=X,NOTIFY=&SYSUID, // REGION=0M

Positional Parameters

After the job statement, there are two positional parameters:

  • Job accounting information — in our example, 504
  • Programmer name field — in our example, SMITH PAYROLL

These positional parameters are not required unless your site has made it a rule.

Keyword Parameters

Then we get to the keyword parameters. Unlike positional parameters, these can go in any order because they all start with keyword= and the value is provided after. The most commonly used keyword parameters are:

CLASS — which JES initiator class the job should run under. Available initiators can be checked by going to the SDSF INIT panel. Sites usually assign initiators to specific batches — for example, class L might be for long-running jobs or class O might be for overnight jobs.

MSGCLASS — where the job output is printed to. Every system should have a class A by default, which points to the JES spool. If your site has other printers set up you may want to code in a different value.

MSGLEVEL — the amount of detail in the job output. Coded as MSGLEVEL=(N1,N2). N1 can be a value from 0–2 and N2 can be a value from 0–1 — the higher the number you specify, the more detail is provided. The system default is (1,1).

TIME — the maximum amount of CPU time (in minutes) the job can use. If the job runs for longer than this, it will be cancelled with an S522 abend.

//        CLASS=X,
//        MSGCLASS=A,
//        MSGLEVEL=(1,1),
//        NOTIFY=&SYSUID,
//        REGION=0M,

IBM Sample Edit Macros

28 May 2025
ispf edit-macros ddnames

IBM provides some sample ISPF edit macros in the SYS1.SISPSAMP library. These are useful as-is or as a basis for learning to write your own edit macros. Today we will discuss a few of them.

First of all, to use the edit macros we need to ensure that SISPSAMP is allocated. This can be done by including it in our login procedures under the SYSPROC concatenation, or with an ALLOC command. For example:

ALLOC F(SYSPROC) DA('SYS1.SISPSAMP') SHR REU

This is a TSO command, so remember to prefix it with TSO if you are entering it from an ISPF panel. Once they are allocated, edit macros are always called by entering the member name on the command line of your ISPF edit session.

ISRONLY

ONLY is an edit macro that combines the functionality of the FIND and EXCLUDE macros. It will display only the lines containing the string that you specify. Instead of doing X ALL;F <string> ALL, you can use:

ONLY <string>

ISRBOX

BOX is an edit macro that inserts a box drawn from characters into the open member you are editing. The box's top left corner will start at your cursor position. It will then reposition your cursor inside the box so you can begin to enter a note in it. It is useful for highlighting notes for yourself or other programmers.

REXX vs CLIST — and Why DDnames Matter

Something is different about these two edit macros — apart from their functionality.

If you look at the members, ISRONLY has a /* REXX */ comment declaration at the top. ISRBOX does not — this is because ISRBOX is a CLIST program. Edit macros can be written in REXX or CLIST, and you will often see a combination of both where CLIST commands are used in a REXX program.

It is important we recognize the difference between the two, because z/OS processes them differently. That is why we allocated SISPSAMP to the SYSPROC concatenation, which can handle running both REXX and CLIST statements. If we were to allocate it to another concatenation like SYSEXEC, which can only process REXX statements, the CLIST macros would return with syntax errors because they are being read as if they are REXX.

This also goes for other DDname concatenations. If you misallocate a panel to ISPMLIB, when it was supposed to be under ISPPLIB, your panels will most likely not display.

ISPF DDname Reference

The base ISPF library types are:

  • ISPMLIB — Message library
  • ISPPLIB — Panel library
  • ISPSLIB — Skeleton library
  • ISPTLIB — Table input library
  • ISPTABL — Table output library
  • ISPFILE — File tailoring output file
  • ISPLLIB — Load module library
  • ISPILIB — Image library

Likewise, TSO uses:

  • SYSPROC — TSO/E CLISTs and REXX execs
  • SYSEXEC — REXX execs only

Getting these mixed up is a common source of mysterious errors when allocating libraries. Always double-check you're allocating to the right DDname for what your library contains.

Macro: Insert job card template
About: An ISREDIT macro to insert a job card into a member open in ISPF edit.
Usage: Allocate the macro to your SYSPROC or SYSEXEC in your login proc or dynamically with:

TSO ALLOC FI(SYSPROC) DA('macro.dataset') SHR REU

Enter the macro name on the command line. Either press Enter to insert at the top of the member, or place your cursor where you would like to insert and then press Enter.

The Macro

/* rexx */
"isredit macro"
"isredit (cur) = cursor"
lineno = cur
line = "//JOBCARD  JOB ,'Name',NOTIFY=&SYSUID.,"
"isredit line_after "lineno" = (line)"
line = "//           MSGCLASS=A,MSGLEVEL=(1,1),CLASS=A"
"isredit line_after "lineno+1" = (line)"
line = "//"
"isredit line_after "lineno+2" = (line)"

The macro inserts three lines: the JOB statement, a continuation line with common parameters, and a blank comment line. Customize the template to match your site's standard job card parameters.

TSO Logon Procedures and RACF

27 March 2025
racf tso logon-procs

SYS1.UADS is the default dataset listing users that are allowed to use TSO/E [1]. Most sites that have RACF or other security products installed use those products to maintain their TSO/E logon information [2]. For a first time installation of RACF, IBM provides a command called RACONVRT to move users from SYS1.UADS to the RACF database [3]. Before you do this, RACF must be set up to protect TSO resources [4].

Once your site is using RACF to manage TSO users (or if your site already is), you can define specific logon procedures for specific users, and allow or disallow users to use certain logon procedures.

Logon Procedures

Say we have a given logon procedure we would like to define — TSLOGP in SYS2.PROCLIB.

At minimum, a logon procedure must have a terminal monitor program (TMP), which is a program that allows a user session to communicate with TSO/E [5]. You may be familiar with the IKJEFT01, IKJEFT1A, and IKJEFT1B TMPs, which can also be used with a JCL job to run commands that you might typically enter in your session in an environment outside of your session — this can keep your screen free so you can keep working if it's a command that will take a long time to execute.

Let's assume the SYS2.PROCLIB(TSLOGP) procedure looks something like this:

//TSLOGP     EXEC PGM=IKJEFT01,DYNAMNBR=20
//SYSIN      DD TERM=TS
//SYSPRINT   DD TERM=TS

This is a minimal logon procedure [6] — it does not define things such as ISPF panels, or other macros or software products. With this logon procedure a user will be limited to working directly from TSO/E.

Like the name of a job in the job card, the first //TSLOGP is the name of our procedure. We are executing IKJEFT01, and the SYSIN and SYSPRINT DDs are both set to the user's terminal session. This allows us to enter TSO commands to IKJEFT01 and for it to return the output to our terminal. The DYNAMNBR param refers to how many datasets you can dynamically allocate at the same time [6] — these are datasets allocated with the TSO ALLOC command, for example.

Defining Logon Procedures to RACF and Permitting Their Use

With your procedure in place, you need to define it to RACF and permit access:

/* Define the procedure to RACF with no universal access */
RDEFINE TSOPROC TSLOGP UACC(NONE)

/* Permit a specific user to use it */
PERMIT TSLOGP CLASS(TSOPROC) ID(<your id>) ACCESS(READ)

/* Refresh the TSOPROC class */
SETROPTS RACLIST(TSOPROC) REFRESH

If you want everyone to be able to use the procedure, use UACC(READ) when defining it and skip the PERMIT step.

After the SETROPTS REFRESH, you should be able to log on with your new procedure. To specify the procedure at logon time, enter it in the Logon Procedure field on the TSO/E logon panel. To set it as a user's default, use the PROC keyword in their RACF TSO segment — see Adding Users to RACF for more on that.

References

  1. IBM — Content and structure of the UADS
  2. IBM — Using the RACF data base to maintain TSO/E users
  3. IBM — Using the RACONVRT command
  4. IBM — Protecting TSO resources
  5. IBM — Executing the terminal monitor program
  6. IBM — Writing a logon procedure

Purging the JES Spool in SDSF

22 February 2025
jes2 sdsf spool

Many mainframe beginners will be familiar with how to manually purge job outputs from the JES spool one by one — that is, accessing the job status log via SDSF;ST and placing a P against the job entry to be purged. But there are ways we can purge multiple jobs without having to manually enter a P against each one.

Most site setups will have automation in place to clear the spool after a given amount of time has passed, but for various reasons we may want to clean up the spool sooner.

Method 1: Purging a Range

Let's consider that we are viewing the SDSF;ST panel with a filter of USER 'our UID' applied. There is a block of multiple job outputs in a row we wish to clear.

To purge a range of job outputs we can place a //P in the action column of the first job in the series, and a // in the last job of the series — much like entering block commands in an ISPF edit session. Hitting Enter will purge the selected job outputs (inclusive) and everything listed between them.

Method 2: JES2 Commands

JES2 commands can be entered the same way most MVS commands are — via the console, or in any SDSF panel prefixed with a /. JES2 commands are also prefixed with a $ to differentiate them from other system and product commands.

The command:

/$POJQ,JM=*

— or just $POJQ,JM=* from a console — will Purge Output from the Job Queue under the Job Mask *. As you may know from other MVS conventions, the wildcard * represents "any". So the above command will purge ALL job outputs. Be careful when issuing this as you may accidentally purge job outputs you didn't mean to.

Luckily, $PO offers many different parameters to target only certain subsections of job outputs. These parameters can also be mixed and matched within the same command to narrow down the subsection even further:

$POJQ,JM=JOB12* — Purge job outputs beginning with the name JOB12 $POJQ,Q=B — Purge job outputs in class B $POJQ,days>2 — Purge job outputs that are older than two days

For a full list of parameters and filtering options, refer to the JES2 Commands reference in the IBM documentation.

1. Copy [`post-template.html`](post-template.html) into `posts/`
2. Fill in the `<!-- EDIT -->` fields (title, date, category, tags, body)
3. Add a post card entry to [`index.html`](index.html) and [`mainframe/index.html`](mainframe/index.html) or [`computing/index.html`](computing/index.html)
